chapter: Averty's letters and Tom Brown's claims
title: Averty's December 1956 letter: Melbourne, Johnny Stein, and Brown's 1951 interview begins
summary: Averty writes from Paris about his travels, correspondence with Stein, Morez and others, and begins quoting Tom Brown's Record Changer story of Frisco and Loretta McDermott and the 1915 Chicago trip.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: This is a letter. Headed Paris, December 16, 1956. Dear Mr. LaRocca, The very long trip I have done through the world is at its end. I am just arrived from Melbourne this morning with a great regret not to have been in New Orleans for meeting you. But fate is blind and can offer me a very next opportunity to go to the States for another film. I suppose you have well received my letter dated November the 11th that I have sent you from Calcutta. If you don't, I will mail you a copy. The 1956 Olympic Games were very uninteresting and Melbourne is an ugly little city of one million and a half inhabitants. I cannot understand why the Olympic Committee could have chosen such a place for the Games! Alva Melbourne has many jazz bands and the musicians know very well of the ODJB music. I have had the pleasure to talk with the leading jazz man of Australia, the leading jazz man of Australia, that's singular, Mr. Graham Bell, spelled G-R-A-E-M-B-E-L-L, and he was very surprised when I have told him that you and I were friends and we exchanged letters. He has asked me your address and I hope he will keep his promise to write you. I hope that we could pursue now a normal correspondence in order to I could begin the writing of my book. I suppose you have been very surprised to read in the Times-Picayune the letter I have sent to Howard Jacobs for asking addresses of some musicians. I thank you to have mailed me the press clipping of this article. As you have read, Mr. Jacobs is not very clever and I think it is really stupid to profit of my awkwardness in English for making laugh his readers. But I should have to read... I beg your pardon. But I should have to read again what I have written and not to put on the paper, quote, jazz lover of Paris, unquote, instead of, quote, jazz lover from Paris, unquote. Now, all of is written in capital letters there and from is underlined. Nevertheless, I have received some interesting letters from Joseph E. Morez, Sr., Bob Coquille, string bass who actually played in New Orleans, and Johnny Stein who lives in New York. Mr. Morez and Mr. Coquille don't tell me many details of historical value, but Mr. Stein has sent me a write-up which appeared in the Downbeat issue of 1938. This article is just the same you have read in fragments in... I believe the word is thee or my. I can't tell. The or my questionnaire I have sent you one year ago. According to your version of the facts, and that I consider as a true version, Mr. Stein maintains a very contestable story. And I intend to send him so many and many questions that he will compel... that he will be compelled, that is, to tell me the truth and to confess he has had a very strange absence of memory. Be sure, Mr. LaRocca, that I shall strive to keep an objective and independent attitude opposite the subsequent declarations of Mr. Johnny Stein, and that I shall not be so stupid and simple for believing all that he will possibly write. But you have to understand that Mr. Stein has a right to tell what he wants, and if his declarations are pure lies, he will be the lone sufferer of his lies, and I shall write in my book that he has disguised the facts for mean things. I suppose that you will agree my attitude, and that you do not believe again that I try to verify what you have told me is true. You perfectly know I believe you for many and many reasons, and that I appreciate the real flavor of sincerity which emanates from all your letters. My lone desire is to oblige the liars who assert to maintain false facts, to recognize and admit their mistakes. As I wrote you in my letter dated November 11th from Calcutta, I prefer that you interview Mr. Harry James by yourself because I believe that you are the lone person by asking him valuable questions about your common past. I am sure that he has a scrapbook, and he will give you many precisions about dates of his venue in New Orleans, about the dancing pair who shot for the first time, quote, jazz it, Mr. LaRocca, exclamation point, unquote, etc. Considering the mistakes I should have done about Tom Brown's band, I pray you to accept my excuses. I should have to write, quote, Brown's band from Dixieland, unquote, according to the Lambert letter. I should like that Mr. Brown writes me, this man prevents me from sleeping, and his lies are astonishing. If I could squeeze his brain like a lemon and analyze the juice, I think that I could know what he has really done in the past. But that thing is impossible, and I pray to you to believe that is a pity. I better read that sentence again. But that thing is impossible, and I pray you to believe that is a pity. Period. Please, Mr. LaRocca, colon, if you meet Mr. Brown, comma, do not talk to him about that crazy thought, exclamation point. In a letter dated July 5th, and that it seems to me you have unfortunately lost, comma, I tried to clear up the Brown's case. Period. I want to copy again what I had wrote about this Brown in this letter, colon, dot, dot, dot, quote. I have read your correspondence about this statement with M. W. Stern, and the prompt end you brought to those false assertions. Period. Nevertheless, comma, Mr. Brown is not only what I suppose he is, a hyphen, a liar, comma, but also a very great imaginative, period. But you know, Mr. LaRocca, that I don't want to bore you in searching the truth about Brown's version, comma, but there is unhappily a precise fact, colon, since Tom Brown has given again in March 1951 an interview to the record changer, comma, his version is still accepted as truth by all the jazz historians, period, and all is written in capital letters. It is certainly a pity, comma, but the things are just like that period, quote. Pardon me. I want you to know what Brown has declared in this issue of the record changer of March 1951, period. You will notice, comma, as I have done, comma, the bitterness and the strange aggressivity of Mr. Brown against you in the ODJB, period. Hear what Mr. Brown declared. Colon, dot, dot, dot, quote, I, comma, Tom Brown was the first, first is capitalized, to take a Dixieland band to Chicago and start this widespread of jazz, period. Everyone else has been doing all the talking about jazz and I have kept still, period. Now it is my turn to talk, period. It all started this way, colon, back in 1913, a group of white musicians was playing regularly at the Young Men's Gymnastic Club dances in New Orleans and on special occasions, the dance team of Frisco and Loretta McDermott, that's capital L-O-R-E-T-T-A, capital N, M-C, capital D-E-R-M-O-T-T, was brought from Chicago to do the show, period. They had a ballroom dancing act and also they did a patsy dance with a lit cigar and dairy by hat, period. Our band played their act so well that Frisco wanted us to go back to Chicago with them at that time, period. I told him that we had quite a few contracts signed, but would consider his offer when these were finished. Then Frisco went back to Chicago and told to Smiley Cabaret of Lams... Smiley Corbett? I'm sorry, Smiley Corbett of Lams. ... ...
